rewritten_text:
When the marriage was celebrated some three weeks afterward, St. Peter's was packed with a veritable crowd of fashionable people. The Dean of Chichester conducted the service most impressively, and everyone declared that no bride and bridegroom had ever made a finer-looking pair. Yet they were something more than handsome: they were happy. Lord Arthur never for an instant regretted anything he had endured for Sybil, while she bestowed upon him the finest gifts a woman can offer a man—adoration, tenderness, and love. Reality did not destroy their romance. They remained young in feeling.

Several years later, after the birth of their two beautiful children, Lady Windermere visited Alton Priory, the charming old property the Duke had given his son on his marriage. One afternoon she sat with Lady Arthur beneath a lime-tree in the garden, watching the little boy and girl flit along the rose-walk like wandering sunbeams. Suddenly she took her hostess's hand and asked, ‘Are you happy, Sybil?’

‘My dear Lady Windermere, naturally I am happy. Are you not?’

‘I haven't time for happiness, Sybil. I always like whoever has most recently been introduced to me; but generally, once I get to know people, they bore me.’

‘Do your lions fail to satisfy you, Lady Windermere?’

‘Oh, entirely! Lions are good for a single season only. Once their manes are clipped, they become the dullest creatures imaginable. And if you are particularly kind to them, they behave atrociously. Do you recall that dreadful Mr. Podgers? An absolute impostor. Naturally that never troubled me, and I forgave him even when he wished to borrow money. But his making love to me was unbearable. He has positively turned me against cheiromancy. Nowadays I occupy myself with telepathy. It is far more entertaining.’

‘You must say nothing against cheiromancy in this house, Lady Windermere. It is the one subject Arthur dislikes hearing joked about. I assure you, he takes it quite seriously.’

‘Surely you don't mean he believes in it, Sybil?’

‘Ask him yourself, Lady Windermere; here he comes.’ Lord Arthur approached through the garden, carrying a great bunch of yellow roses, with his two children dancing around him.

‘Lord Arthur?’

‘Yes, Lady Windermere?’

‘Surely you cannot mean that you believe in cheiromancy?’

‘Certainly I do,’ the young man answered with a smile.

‘But why?’

‘Because I owe it every happiness in my life,’ he murmured, dropping into a wicker chair.

‘No one raising you by hand then. Not at all!’

Joe offered me more gravy, but I was afraid to accept it.

‘He gave you a world of trouble, ma'am,’ said Mrs. Hubble, sympathizing with my sister.

‘Trouble?’ my sister repeated. ‘Trouble?’ Then she launched into a dreadful list of all the illnesses I had been guilty of, all the nights I had wickedly stayed awake, all the high places I had fallen from and the low places I had fallen into, every injury I had done myself, and every time she had wished me in my grave and I had stubbornly refused to go.

I think the Romans must have irritated one another terribly with their noses. Perhaps that explains why they were such restless people. At any rate, Mr. Wopsle's Roman nose annoyed me so much during the account of my misdeeds that I wanted to pull it until he howled. Yet everything I had suffered so far was nothing beside the terrible feelings that came over me when the silence following my sister's account was broken. Throughout that silence, as I was painfully aware, everyone had stared at me with anger and disgust.

‘Still,’ said Mr. Pumblechook, gently guiding the company back to the subject they had wandered from, ‘pork, when it's boiled, is rich too, isn't it?’

‘Have a little brandy, Uncle,’ said my sister.

Oh heavens, the moment had finally come! He would notice it was weak, he would say so, and I would be ruined. With both hands, I gripped the table leg beneath the cloth and waited for my fate.

My sister fetched the stone bottle, returned with it, and poured him some brandy. Nobody else took any. The wretched man played with his glass, picking it up, holding it to the light, and setting it down again, stretching out my torment. All the while, Mrs. Joe and Joe were busily clearing the table for the pie and pudding.

I could not stop watching him. Still clinging to the table leg with both hands and feet, I saw the miserable creature toy with his glass, lift it, smile, tip his head back, and swallow the brandy. Instantly the whole company was struck with utter alarm. He leapt to his feet, spun around several times in a dreadful, jerking dance of whooping coughs, and rushed out the door. Then we could see him through the window, lunging about and spitting violently, pulling hideous faces and apparently out of his mind.

I kept holding tight while Mrs. Joe and Joe ran to help him.

‘My nerves can't stand that sort of thing.’

‘But could you really feel comfortable spending the whole evening away from the poor boy?’

‘Yes. His father can, you see, so why shouldn't I? Jemima is very careful, and she could send us news of him every hour. I really think Charles might as well have told his father we would all come. I'm no more worried about little Charles now than he is. I was terribly frightened yesterday, but things are very different today.’

‘Well, if you think there's still time to let them know, why don't you go with your husband? Leave little Charles with me. Mr. and Mrs. Musgrove can't object while I'm here to look after him.’

‘Do you mean it?’ cried Mary, her eyes lighting up. ‘Goodness, what a very good idea! An excellent idea, really. Certainly I might as well go, since I'm no use at home, am I? Staying only upsets me. You don't have a mother's feelings, so you're much better suited to it. You can get little Charles to do anything; he always obeys you straight away. That will be far better than leaving him with only Jemima. Oh, I shall definitely go. I'm sure I ought to if I can, just as much as Charles should, because they're so eager for me to meet Captain Wentworth. And I know you don't mind being left alone. What an excellent thought, Anne! I'll tell Charles and get ready at once. You can send for us immediately if anything goes wrong, you know. But I expect there will be nothing to worry you. You may be quite sure I wouldn't go if I weren't completely at ease about my dear child.’

A moment later she was knocking at her husband's dressing-room door. Anne followed her upstairs in time to hear the entire conversation, which Mary began in a triumphant voice.

‘I'm coming with you, Charles, because I'm no more useful at home than you are. Even if I shut myself up with the child forever, I couldn't make him do anything he didn't want to. Anne will stay. She's offered to remain at home and look after him. It was Anne's own suggestion, so I shall come with you, which will be much better. I haven't dined at the other house since Tuesday.’

‘That's very kind of Anne,’ her husband replied, ‘and I'd be very pleased to have you come. But it does seem rather unfair that she should be left at home alone to nurse our sick child.’
